questions.question: (i) What do you mean by "begging the question"? (ii) Is the following argument correct? It supposedly shows that is an even integer whenever is an even integer. Suppose that is even. Then for some integer . Let for some integer . This shows that is even. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• (a) What do you mean by “begging the question”? . . . [A]/[CO1]
  • • Begging the question is a logical fallacy in which the conclusion of an argument is assumed in one of its premises instead of being proved. Thus, the argument is circular and provides no independent evidence for the conclusion. . . . 2 Marks (b) Is the following argument correct? It supposedly shows that n is an even integer whenevern2 is an even integer. Suppose that n2 is even. Then n2 = 2k for some integer k. Let n = 2l for some integerl. This shows that n is even.
  • • No, the argument is incorrect. The statement n = 2l is assumed without jus- tiﬁcation. This is precisely what needs to be proved. Hence, the proof commits the fallacy of begging the question . . . 4 Marks

questions.question: (i) What is meant by a direct proof? (ii) Give a direct proof to show that the sum of two even integers is even. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• (a) What is meant by a direct proof? . . . [A]/[CO1]
  • • A direct proof is a method of proving a statement by assuming that the given hypothesis is true and using deﬁnitions, axioms, and previously established results to logically deduce the conclusion. . . . 2 Marks (b) Give a direct proof to show that the sum of two even integers is even.
  • • a = 2m and b = 2n. Therefore, a +b = 2m + 2n = 2(m +n). Since m +n is an integer, let k =m +n. Then a +b = 2k, where k is an integer. Hence, a +b is even. Therefore, the sum of two even integers is even. . . . 4 Marks
